blocks.text: So much for the Greek interpreters of the word bath-jaana. I now turn to the Chaldeans, Syrians, and Arabs, who all follow the same view. For the three Chaldee versions, Onkelos, Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum, have here נעמא naama, or נעמיתא naamitha. The Syriac also has ܢܥܡܐ naama. And the Arabic versions, both printed and manuscript, have نعام [naʿām] naam, or نعامة [naʿāma] naama. That these words signify the ostrich is as certain as anything can be. This the Arab lexicographers, historians, geographers, physicians and philosophers teach me with one consent. But above all Damir and Alkazuinius, who in their chapters On the naam, or naama, describe the ostrich far more accurately than the Greek and Roman writers. And Abenbitar, who under naama reproduces word for word what Galen has on the ostrich in book 3 On Foods. Indeed, the same writers also explain the reason for the name. The ostrich and the camel have much in common. Accordingly the foot of each is called خف [khuff] choph, and منسم [mansim] mensim: and the female of each قلوص [qalūṣ] kalus. Thus نعام [naʿām] naam, and نعم [naʿam] naam are close to each other: the former signifies the ostrich, the latter the camel. Hence [II, 819] it is that ظربان [ẓarbān] dorban, that is, the species of weasel which barbarous writers call putorium [polecat] from its stench, is said by the Arabs to be مفرق النعم [mufarriq al-naʿam] the disperser of the naam, because with its stench it scatters and disperses the herds of camels. And in the plural انعام [anʿām] anam are camels. As in these words of the Muslim theologians in Alcamus: الله جعل لكم الانعام لتركبوا [Allāh jaʿala lakum al-anʿām li-tarkabū] God has made for you the Alanama (camels), that you might ride on them. Therefore the ostrich too is called نعام [naʿām] naam, because it resembles the camel. Similar is what Algiahid observes, that the ostrich is called by the Persians استرموك [ushtarmurgh] istarmuch, as if you were to say camel-bird, because it seems to be an animal compounded of both. Hence Alkazuinius: نعامة حيوان مركب من حلقة الطير والجمل اخذ من البعير العنق والمنسم ومن الطير المنقار والجناح والريش [naʿāma ḥayawān murakkab min ḥalqat al-ṭayr wa-l-jamal akhadha min al-baʿīr al-ʿunuq wa-l-mansim wa-min al-ṭayr al-minqār wa-l-janāḥ wa-l-rīsh] The ostrich is an animal composed of the nature of the camel and of the bird: from the camel it took its neck and feet; from the bird its beak, wings and feathers. So, as in Greek and Latin, so too in Persian, in Chaldee, in Syriac and in Arabic, the name of this bird was given by ἡ μεμιγμένη φύσις τῷ χερσαίῳ ζώῳ [hē memigmenē physis tō chersaiō zōō]. And when the more recent lexicographers of the Chaldee language interpret נעמא naama, or נעמיתא naamitha, as owl or eagle owl, they commit a grave error, into which they would never have fallen had they possessed even the slightest [col. 224] knowledge of the Arabic language. Though they need not have gone so far. For it is clear from the Talmud as well that נעמית naamith is the ostrich. Thus in the tractate Kelim, or On Vessels, ch. 17, §. 14, there is listed among vessels ביצת נעמית המצופה, a naamith egg overlaid (that is, with gold or silver). It is certain that the naamith egg is the egg of the ostrich, from which vessels are made, a very well-known fact. Pliny, book 10, chapter 1: Their eggs (of ostriches) are, because of their size, regarded by some as vessels. And of the same Lucian in The Dipsads: Σκεύεσι χρῶνται κενώσαντες, καὶ ἐκπώματα ποιοῦνται ἐπ᾽ αὐτῶν· [Skeuesi chrōntai kenōsantes, kai ekpōmata poiountai ep᾽ autōn] When emptied they use them as vessels, and cups are made of them. Again in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 18, fol. 128a: מטלטלין שברי זכוכית מפני שמאכל לנעמיות, They may carry about (lawfully on the Sabbath day) fragments of glass, because they are food for ostriches. That is certainly how the word לנעמיות should be translated, not owls or eagle owls, which nobody bothers to keep at home; to say nothing of their being carnivorous birds, whereas the ostrich swallows without discrimination whatever is offered it: iron, bones, linen, glass, stones. This would be very easy to prove from Pliny, Aelian, Damir, Alkazuinius, Leo Africanus, Marmol and others.
